1	# OEE — the three components and the traps
2	
3	Load this before computing anything.
4	
5	**OEE is the number everyone in operations knows by heart.** A plant reporting
6	60–70% is normal; 85% is world-class. That familiarity is exactly why a wrong OEE
7	destroys trust in the whole report — a supervisor who sees 91% on a bad week
8	stops reading.
9	
10	```
11	OEE = Availability × Performance × Quality
12	```
13	
14	---
15	
16	## Never report the composite alone
17	
18	**Always show the three components separately.** This is a done-when condition,
19	not a presentation preference.
20	
21	An OEE of 62% caused by availability is a maintenance problem. The same 62%
22	caused by quality is a completely different meeting with different people in it.
23	The composite tells a plant manager the day was bad; the components tell them who
24	to call.
25	
26	---
27	
28	## Availability
29	
30	```
31	Availability = run time / planned production time
32	```
33	
34	**Planned production time is a configured definition, not a derivation.**
35	`onboarding` captures it per site: scheduled shift hours minus whatever that plant
36	excludes — planned maintenance windows, breaks, scheduled changeovers. Read it
37	from the `## Plant context` block and **state the definition in the report**, because
38	two plants computing availability against different denominators are not
39	comparable and neither is one plant before and after a definition change.
40	
41	### Four denominator traps
42	
43	**Unscheduled overtime.** A machine that ran hours it was never scheduled for can
44	produce run time exceeding planned production time, and availability above 100%.
45	**Report it; do not clamp it to 100%.** An availability of 118% is a finding
46	about the schedule definition, and silently capping it hides both the overtime
47	and the definitional problem.
48	
49	**Cross-midnight shifts.** A three-shift plant has a shift that starts on one
50	calendar day and ends on the next. The `production_day` attribution rule is
51	configured per site — the day the shift started, or the day it ended — and the
52	report states which convention is in use. Getting it wrong moves a whole shift of
53	output to the wrong day, which makes one day look bad and the next look good.
54	
55	**Planned downtime counted as downtime.** A scheduled PM window is excluded from
56	the denominator, not counted as a stoppage. Counting it as unavailability
57	punishes a plant for doing maintenance correctly.
58	
59	**A machine idle because there was nothing to run.** This is real, common, and
60	not a maintenance problem. Whether the plant excludes no-demand time from planned
61	production time is their definitional choice, captured at onboarding. Do not
62	decide it here.
63	
64	---
65	
66	## Performance
67	
68	```
69	Performance = (ideal cycle time × total count) / run time
70	```
71	
72	Ideal cycle time comes from the routing's standard time for the operation.
73	Where a plant's routing standards are stale or absent, **performance cannot be
74	computed** — see the rule below.
75	
76	Performance above 100% means the part ran faster than its standard, which
77	usually means the standard is wrong rather than the machine being miraculous.
78	Report it as a finding about the standard.
79	
80	---
81	
82	## Quality
83	
84	```
85	Quality = good count / total count
86	```
87	
88	Total count is good plus scrap plus rework, per the plant's own convention.
89	**Rework is the ambiguous one** — a part reworked into conformance was not made
90	right the first time, so first-pass yield excludes it. State which convention was
91	used, on every run, as one line under the table:
92	
93	- Export has a rework column → *quality = good ÷ (good + scrap + rework),
94	  first-pass yield.*
95	- Export has no rework column → *quality = good ÷ (good + scrap); no rework
96	  column, so first-pass yield could not be applied.*
97	
98	The caveat belongs to the second case only. Printing "no rework column"
99	against an export that has one is a false statement about the plant's data.
100	
101	---
102	
103	## The rule that matters most: never substitute 1.0 for a missing component
104	
105	If a component cannot be computed, **report the components you have and say the
106	composite is unavailable.** Do not multiply by 1.0 in place of the missing one.
107	
108	This is `../../../shared/absent-is-not-zero.md` applied to the most-watched number
109	in the plant, and it fails in the flattering direction. A plant with no routing
110	standards, whose performance is therefore unknown, would report:
111	
112	```
113	Availability 0.78 × Performance [unknown as 1.0] × Quality 0.96 = 75%
114	```
115	
116	That 75% looks like a decent day and it is arithmetic on a value nobody measured.
117	Real performance of 0.71 would have made it 53%. **Absent is not zero, and absent
118	is also not one hundred percent.**
119	
120	The honest output:
121	
122	> *"Availability 78%, quality 96%. Performance can't be computed — the routing
123	> standards for these parts aren't in the dataset, so there's no ideal cycle time
124	> to compare against. Composite OEE is unavailable until those land."*
125	
126	---
127	
128	## Grain
129	
130	Compute per asset or per line, and **state which**. An OEE averaged across a cell
131	of five machines hides the one machine causing the problem, which is usually the
132	entire point of looking.
133	
134	Where the plant's vocabulary calls it a cell, a line or a work center, use their
135	word, per the `## Plant context` block.
136	
137	---
138	
139	## Sanity checks before reporting
140	
141	| Check | If it fails |
142	|---|---|
143	| Each component within 0–100% | Report the value and the likely denominator cause. Never clamp |
144	| Composite within 0–100% | Follows from the components; a composite outside range means one is wrong |
145	| Total count equals good plus scrap plus rework | Report the discrepancy; it means two sources disagree |
146	| Run time not greater than planned produ...[truncated]

1	# The reschedule proposal — and where it stops
2	
3	Load this before proposing any schedule move.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## What this is not
8	
9	**This is not finite-capacity scheduling.**
10	
11	Producing an optimal shop schedule is a constraint-optimisation problem. A
12	language model asked to do it will return a plausible-looking schedule that
13	quietly violates constraints — and that is **worse than returning nothing**,
14	because a scheduler who accepts it discovers the violation on the floor, at
15	which point the report has actively caused a problem it was supposed to report.
16	
17	So there is a hard line here, and it is drawn deliberately rather than
18	apologetically.
19	
20	| Out of scope | In scope |
21	|---|---|
22	| Re-optimising the day | One or two specific moves |
23	| Sequencing every job across every cell | Moving one job, and tracing what that displaces |
24	| Balancing load across the plant | Naming what still misses its date after the move |
25	| Anything presented as optimal | Something presented as checked, with the checks listed |
26	
27	---
28	
29	## What a proposal must contain
30	
31	Four parts. A proposal missing any of them is not actionable and should not be
32	offered.
33	
34	1. **The move.** Specific: which job, from where, to where — and **the
35	   changeover it implies**: what the receiving cell was running before, and
36	   what switching it costs. A move that reads as free because nobody named
37	   the changeover is not a checked move.
38	2. **What it displaces.** Every job the move pushes, and where each one lands.
39	3. **What still misses.** After the move, which commitments are still not met.
40	   **A proposal that claims nothing misses is the one to distrust most.**
41	4. **What was checked, and what was not.** Explicitly. This is what lets a
42	   scheduler accept or reject without rebuilding the analysis.
43	
44	An example, with the changeover made explicit:
45	
46	> *"Run 4471 on cell B instead of cell A; cell B was running 4390's finishing
47	> pass, so this costs a changeover — call it 40 minutes on this tooling. That
48	> pushes 4402 to second shift, where it still makes its date; 4390 now misses
49	> by one day."*
50	
51	Four clauses. One move with its changeover, one displacement with its
52	outcome, one casualty named. That is the whole deliverable. Where the
53	changeover cost genuinely can't be estimated, say that explicitly rather than
54	silently dropping it — it is degradation, per the table below, not omission.
55	
56	---
57	
58	## The honesty requirement
59	
60	**State what was not checked.** A move traced through due dates but not through
61	tooling availability, operator certification, or material on hand is a partial
62	check, and saying so is what keeps it useful.
63	
64	> *"Checked: due dates on the three affected jobs, and cell B's routing for 4471.
65	> Not checked: whether cell B has the fixture, whether second shift has a
66	> certified operator for 4402, and material availability. Worth confirming those
67	> before committing."*
68	
69	A scheduler reading that knows exactly how much of their own judgment is still
70	required. A scheduler reading a bare proposal does not, and will either
71	over-trust it or ignore it.
72	
73	---
74	
75	## One or two moves, not a plan
76	
77	Propose per significant exception, not for the day as a whole. Where three
78	exceptions each need a move and the moves interact, **say that they interact and
79	stop** rather than composing them into a schedule.
80	
81	> *"These three exceptions all want cell B. Individually each move works; together
82	> they conflict, and untangling that is a scheduling decision rather than
83	> something I can check. Here are the three moves separately, with the conflict
84	> named."*
85	
86	---
87	
88	## Never applied
89	
90	The proposal is **drafted for the scheduler**, never applied to any system. This
91	skill writes nothing to a system of record. It reports, prices, and proposes.
92	
93	---
94	
95	## Degradation
96	
97	The proposal depends on the schedule export and on changeover or routing data.
98	
99	| Available | Behavior |
100	|---|---|
101	| Schedule export and routing data | Propose the move, fully traced |
102	| Schedule export, no routing or changeover data | Propose the move; state that changeover time was not accounted for |
103	| Neither | **Report the exception with its impact on commitments and no proposed move — and say which** |
104	
105	That last row is the important one. Per `../../../shared/absent-is-not-zero.md`,
106	the report says the move was not proposed because the schedule data was not
107	available. It does not silently omit the proposal, which reads as "nothing needed
108	to move."

1	# Computed figures — a number is printed, never retyped
2	
3	**Shared across the plugin.** Every skill that reports a number follows this.
4	
5	The failure this exists to stop has one shape. The skill does the work
6	correctly, then writes the summary from memory. The summary says "eleven
7	maintenance records" where the data holds six, "3.1× the control limit" where
8	the division gives 2.36, "five orders" where the file has six — the customer's
9	own order being the one missed. Each figure is stated with total confidence,
10	and each is the first thing a quality manager or an estimator will check.
11	
12	A second shape sits next to it: the confident absence. "The sister machine has
13	no bearing history." "There is no PM plan in the library." Said after one
14	search, about a record that was there.
15	
16	---
17	
18	## The rule
19	
20	**Every count, total, ratio, percentage and "N of M" in user-facing output is
21	produced by code run over the data in this session, and printed from that
22	result. A number is never retyped, rounded from memory, or paraphrased.**
23	
24	**A negative claim — "has no history," "no plan exists," "not in the file" —
25	cites the exact query or filter that returned nothing.** Where the search tool
26	may be incomplete (SharePoint search under-reports), enumerate the folder
27	instead, or say *"not found by search"* rather than *"does not exist."* Those
28	are different claims and only the first one was earned.
29	
30	---
31	
32	## The figures block — a required part of the output
33	
34	A rule that says "check your numbers" is a rule nobody can see being skipped.
35	So the check is an output, not an intention.
36	
37	**Every run that reports a number emits a figures block**, produced by code,
38	before the prose that uses it. One row per figure:
39	
40	| Figure | Value | Computed from | Filter or query |
41	|---|---|---|---|
42	| Maintenance records, HAAS-VF4-02 | 9 | maintenance export | `asset_id == "HAAS-VF4-02"` |
43	| Sibling records mentioning "bearing" | 2 (LMB-13781, LMB-14022, both HAAS-VF4-05) | maintenance export | same model, `notes` contains "bearing" |
44	| Measured ÷ upper control limit | 1.87 | inspection export | measured and limit both from the same computation |
45	| PM plan documents found | 0 — **not found by search** | M365 library | search "PM plan"; folder not enumerated |
46	
47	Then three things hold, and a reader can check all three without re-running
48	anything:
49	
50	1. **The prose quotes the block.** A number that appears in the narrative, a
51	   table or a headline appears in the block with the same value. A number in
52	   the prose with no row in the block is a defect.
53	2. **A ratio comes from the same computation as its parts.** Do not compute a
54	   control limit in code and then divide by it in your head.
55	3. **A subtotal reconciles to its total in the block itself.** If 126 records
56	   matched, the exact and normalized rows add to 126, and each equals the sum
57	   of the classes it is made of. A block that does not add up is fixed before
58	   anything is written from it.
59	
60	Where the skill already emits "the structured data behind the report," the
61	figures block is part of it. Where the output is a controlled document going to
62	a customer or supplier, the block stays on the internal side.
63	
64	---
65	
66	## When no code can be run
67	
68	Some sessions have no code execution. Then the count was made by reading, and
69	the output says so: **"counted by reading, not computed — verify before
70	relying on it,"** on the block and beside any figure that matters. Never
71	present a hand count as a computed one. This is `absent-is-not-zero.md` applied
72	to the method rather than the data: an unverified number named as unverified is
73	useful, and one dressed as computed is worse than none.
74	
75	---
76	
77	## What this does not change
78	
79	- A figure that cannot be read is still reported unreadable. The block carries
80	  the row with the reason, never a guess.
81	- Rates, whether read from an `MFG_*` variable or the plant profile, follow
82	  `secret-config.md`. The block names the source; the value appears only where
83	  the audience rule allows.
84	- Computing a figure is not applying a fix. Anything that changes data still
85	  needs its yes.

r in routing} pn_wo = {r["part_number"] for r in wos} fig("Part numbers in plan not in output", sorted(pn_plan - pn_out) or "none", "plan.csv vs output.csv", "set difference, exact match") fig("Part I've written the morning report to `out/report-output/morning-report.html`. It covers SITE-1 for production day **12 Nov 2026**, because that is the newest day in the drop.

**The data is 3 days old.** There's no output, plan or downtime for 13 or 14 Nov, so I can't confirm whether the late work orders were finished since.

| | 12 Nov |
|---|---|
| Good output against plan | 1,000 of 1,050 (95.2%, 50 short). Total including scrap was 1,015 |
| OEE | 81.7%: availability 95.5%, performance 86.8%, quality 98.5% |
| Downtime | 65 min over 2 events. By minutes: tool change overrun on CNC-01 (45 min), then waiting on material on CNC-02 (20 min). By frequency they're tied at one event each, and both events had a usable reason code |
| Scrap | 15 units, 80% of them PN-100 |

**Losses are not priced.** There's no downtime cost rate and no standard cost per part in the drop. The finance memo has shop rates, but not for "VMC", the work centre these exports use, and a shop rate isn't a downtime cost. I left the dollar figures as unknown rather than $0.

**Decisions needed today:**
1. **WO-1002** (PN-200) is 30 short and was due 13 Nov. I drafted one make-up move for the scheduler (about 62 min on CNC-02); it isn't applied.
2. **WO-1001** (PN-100) is 20 short and was due 14 Nov. Its draft move is about 23 min on CNC-01.
3. Someone needs to set a downtime cost rate and give a standard cost for PN-100 and PN-200.

**Worth looking into:**
- **Performance is the biggest loss.** About 182 run-minutes aren't explained by the routing standards, almost three times the logged downtime. Either the standards are off or short stops aren't being logged.
- **Find out why the 13–14 Nov exports didn't arrive.**

I can't tell the impact on customer orders, because the work order export has no sales order link. Nothing was posted or written to any system. Save the page over yesterday's.
